In [[statistics]] and [[econometrics]], '''extremum estimators''' are a wide [[class (mathematics)|class]] of [[estimator]]s for [[parametric model]]s that are calculated through maximization (or minimization) of a certain [[objective function]], which depends on the data. The general theory of extremum estimators was developed by {{harvtxt|Amemiya|1985}}.

== Definition ==
An estimator <math style="vertical-align:0">\scriptstyle\hat\theta</math> is called an '''extremum estimator''', if there is an ''objective function'' <math style="vertical-align:-.35em">\scriptstyle\hat{Q}_n</math> such that
: <math>
    \hat\theta = \underset{\theta\in\Theta}{\operatorname{arg\;max}}\ \widehat{Q}_n(\theta),
  </math>
where Θ is the [[parameter space]]. Sometimes a slightly weaker definition is given:
: <math>
    \widehat Q_n(\hat\theta) \geq  \max_{\theta\in\Theta}\,\widehat Q_n(\theta) - o_p(1),
  </math>
where ''o''<sub>''p''</sub>(1) is the variable [[small o in probability notation|converging in probability to zero]]. With this modification <math style="vertical-align:0">\scriptstyle\hat\theta</math> doesn't have to be the exact maximizer of the objective function, just be sufficiently close to it.

The theory of extremum estimators does not specify what the objective function should be. There are [[#Examples|various types]] of objective functions suitable for different models, and this framework allows us to analyse the theoretical properties of such estimators from a unified perspective. The theory only specifies the properties that the objective function has to possess, and so selecting a particular objective function only requires verifying that those properties are satisfied.

== Consistency ==
[[File:Ee noncompactness.svg|thumb|240px|When the parameter space Θ is not compact ({{nowrap|Θ {{=}} [[Real line|'''R''']]}} in this example), then even if the objective function is uniquely maximized at ''θ''<sub>0</sub>, this maximum may be not well-separated, in which case the estimator <math style="vertical-align:0">\scriptscriptstyle\hat\theta</math> will fail to be consistent.]]

If the parameter space Θ is [[compact set|compact]] and there is a ''limiting function'' ''Q''<sub>0</sub>(''θ'') such that: <math style="vertical-align:-.35em">\scriptstyle\hat{Q}_n(\theta)</math> converges to ''Q''<sub>0</sub>(''θ'') [[convergence in probability|in probability]] uniformly over Θ, and the function ''Q''<sub>0</sub>(''θ'') is [[continuous function|continuous]] and has a unique maximum at ''θ'' = ''θ''<sub>0</sub> then <math style="vertical-align:0">\scriptstyle\hat\theta</math> is '''[[consistent estimator|consistent]]''' for ''θ''<sub>0</sub>.<ref>Newey & McFadden (1994), Theorem 2.1</ref>

The [[uniform convergence in probability]] of <math style="vertical-align:-.35em">\scriptstyle\hat{Q}_n(\theta)</math> means that
: <math>
    \sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \big| \hat{Q}_n(\theta) - Q_0(\theta) \big| \ \xrightarrow{p}\ 0.
  </math>

The requirement for Θ to be compact can be replaced with a weaker assumption that the maximum of ''Q''<sub>0</sub> was well-separated, that is there should not exist any points ''θ'' that are distant from ''θ''<sub>0</sub> but such that ''Q''<sub>0</sub>(''θ'') were close  to ''Q''<sub>0</sub>(''θ''<sub>0</sub>). Formally, it means that for any sequence {''θ<sub>i</sub>''} such that {{nowrap|''Q''<sub>0</sub>(''θ<sub>i</sub>'') → ''Q''<sub>0</sub>(''θ''<sub>0</sub>)}}, it should be true that {{nowrap|''θ<sub>i</sub>'' → ''θ''<sub>0</sub>}}.

== Asymptotic normality ==

Assuming that consistency has been established and the derivatives of the sample <math>Q_{n}</math> satisfy some other conditions,<ref>{{cite web |first=Xiaoxia |last=Shi |title=Lecture Notes: Asymptotic Normality of Extremum Estimators |url=https://www.ssc.wisc.edu/~xshi/econ715/Lecture_4_normality.pdf }}</ref> the extremum estimator converges to an asymptotically Normal distribution.

== Examples ==
{{unordered list
|1= [[Maximum likelihood estimation]] uses the objective function
: <math>
    \hat{Q}_n(\theta) = \log \left[ \prod_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i|\theta) \right] = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log f(x_i|\theta) ,
  </math>
where ''f''(·{{!}}''θ'') is the [[probability density function|density function]] of the distribution from where the observations are drawn. This objective function is called the [[likelihood function|log-likelihood function]].<ref>{{cite book |first=Fumio |last=Hayashi |author-link=Fumio Hayashi |title=Econometrics |location=Princeton |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2000 |isbn=0-691-01018-8 |page=448 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QyIW8WUIyzcC&pg=PA448 }}</ref>

|2= [[Generalized method of moments]] estimator is defined through the objective function
: <math>
    \hat{Q}_n(\theta) = - \Bigg(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g(x_i,\theta)\Bigg)' \hat{W}_n \Bigg(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g(x_i,\theta)\Bigg),
  </math>
where ''g''(·{{!}}''θ'') is the ''moment condition'' of the model.<ref>{{cite book |first=Fumio |last=Hayashi |author-link=Fumio Hayashi |title=Econometrics |location=Princeton |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2000 |isbn=0-691-01018-8 |page=447 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QyIW8WUIyzcC&pg=PA447 }}</ref>

|3= [[Minimum distance estimation|Minimum distance]] estimator
|4= [[Least squares]] estimator
}}
